test-one-proportion-s1.title: A mentoring program and chronic absence
test-one-proportion-s1.text: Last year, 18% of a large school district's students were chronically absent (missed 10% or more of school days). This year the district started a mentoring program and wants to know whether the proportion has gone down. A researcher selects a random sample of 450 of the district's 21,000 students; 63 of them are chronically absent so far. She tests $H_0: p = 0.18$ against $H_a: p < 0.18$ at $\alpha = 0.05$, where $p$ is the true proportion of all the district's students who are chronically absent this year.

test-one-proportion-s2.title: Computer output: a four-day school week
test-one-proportion-s2.text: A polling firm selects a random sample of 1,000 adults in a state and asks whether they would support a four-day school week. The firm wants to know whether more than half of the state's adults support it. Its software prints the output below.

table.caption: Test and confidence interval for one proportion (invented data)

items.q: Calculate the test statistic. Give two decimal places.

mistakes.why: That uses $\hat{p} = 0.14$ in the standard deviation. A test uses $p_0 = 0.18$: $\sqrt{0.18(0.82)/450}$.
The sign is backward: statistic minus null value is $0.14 - 0.18$, a negative number.

items.q: Find the p-value. Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That doubles the tail as for a two-sided test. $H_a: p < 0.18$ is one-sided: use one tail.
That is the right tail. "Less than" means the area to the left of $z = -2.21$.

why.correct: $H_a: p < 0.18$, so the p-value is the left tail: $P(Z \le -2.21) = 0.0136$. Technology (a 1-proportion z test) gives $z = -2.21$ and p-value 0.0136.

items.q: State the conclusion of the test at $\alpha = 0.05$.

conclude.parameter: the true proportion of all the district's students who are chronically absent this year

options: There is convincing evidence
There is not convincing evidence
It is proven

why.1: The p-value is below $\alpha$, so the evidence is convincing.
why.2: A test gives evidence; it never proves.

options: is less than 0.18
is greater than 0.18
is equal to 0.18

why.2: Evidence is always for $H_a$, never that $H_0$ is true.

options: that the true proportion of all the district's students who are chronically absent this year
that the proportion of the 450 sampled students who are chronically absent
that the mentoring program lowered the proportion of chronically absent students, which

why.1: The sample proportion is known to be 0.14; the conclusion is about the population.
why.2: This study has no comparison group, so it cannot show the program caused a change.

conclude.model: Because the p-value of 0.0136 is less than α = 0.05, we reject H0. There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of all the district's students who are chronically absent this year is less than 0.18.

why.correct: Because $0.0136 < 0.05$, reject $H_0$. The conclusion is about the parameter, in context, with evidence language and the direction of $H_a$.

items.q: Suppose the researcher had chosen $\alpha = 0.01$ before collecting the data. What would she conclude?
options: Reject $H_0$, because the p-value is small
Fail to reject $H_0$: not convincing evidence that $p < 0.18$
Accept $H_0$: the true proportion is 0.18
Change to $\alpha = 0.05$ so the result is significant

why.correct: Because $0.0136 > 0.01$, she would fail to reject $H_0$: there would not be convincing evidence at the 1% level that the true proportion is less than 0.18. That does not mean the proportion is 0.18.
options: At $\alpha = 0.01$, the p-value 0.0136 is not small enough: it is greater than 0.01.
A test never accepts $H_0$; failing to reject means the evidence is not strong enough.
The significance level is fixed before the data; changing it afterward to get a result is not allowed.

items.q: Based on this study, can the district conclude that the mentoring program caused the drop in chronic absence?
options: Yes, because the p-value of 0.0136 is less than the significance level of 0.05
Yes, because the 450 students were chosen at random
No, because a significance test is not meant for data about schools
No: with no randomly assigned comparison group, other changes could explain it

why.correct: The test gives evidence that the proportion this year is below 18%, but the study is not an experiment: there was no randomly assigned comparison group, and other things changed from last year to this year. It shows a change, not its cause.
options: A small p-value shows the change is unlikely to be chance; it cannot show what caused it.
Random sampling lets her generalize to the district; it does not create a comparison group.
Tests work for any random sample; the problem here is the design, not the subject.
Right: only random assignment to treatments supports a cause-and-effect conclusion.

items.q: Which hypotheses did the software test, where $p$ is the true proportion of all the state's adults who would support a four-day week?

why.correct: The output line "p = 0.5 vs p > 0.5" gives $H_0: p = 0.5$ and $H_a: p > 0.5$: one-sided, matching "more than half".
options: Right: read the test line of the output.
The null value is 0.5 from the question. 0.532 is the sample proportion.
The output says "p > 0.5", and the question asks about more than half: one-sided.
Hypotheses are about $p$, never about $\hat{p}$.

items.q: The firm had chosen $\alpha = 0.01$. State the conclusion.

conclude.parameter: the true proportion of all the state's adults who would support a four-day school week

options: There is not convincing evidence
There is convincing evidence
There is proof

why.1: The p-value, 0.0215, is above $\alpha = 0.01$, so the evidence is not convincing at this level.

options: is greater than 0.5
is equal to 0.5
is less than 0.5

why.1: Failing to reject does not show the proportion equals 0.5. The conclusion still names the alternative: "not convincing evidence that ... is greater than 0.5".

options: that the true proportion of all the state's adults who would support a four-day school week
that the 532 adults in the sample
that the sample proportion of 0.532

why.1: The conclusion is about the population, not the sampled adults.
why.2: We know the sample proportion is 0.532; the conclusion is about $p$.

conclude.model: Because the p-value of 0.0215 is greater than α = 0.01, we fail to reject H0. There is not convincing evidence that the true proportion of all the state's adults who would support a four-day school week is greater than 0.5.

why.correct: Because $0.0215 > 0.01$, fail to reject $H_0$. The data do not give convincing evidence, at the 1% level, that more than half of the state's adults support a four-day week. This does not show that the true proportion is 0.5.

items.q: If the firm had used $\alpha = 0.05$ instead, which conclusion would be correct?
options: Reject $H_0$: convincing evidence that more than half of adults support it
Reject $H_0$: the test proves that exactly 53.2% of the state's adults support it
Fail to reject $H_0$, because 0.532 is close to 0.5
Reject $H_0$: the sample proportion is greater than 0.5

why.correct: Because $0.0215 < 0.05$, reject $H_0$: there is convincing evidence that the true proportion of all the state's adults who would support a four-day week is greater than 0.5.
options: A test gives evidence, never proof, and 0.532 is the sample result, not the population value.
Compare the p-value with $\alpha$, not the sample proportion with 0.5 by eye.
We already knew that. The conclusion is about the population proportion.

items.q: The software also gives a 90% confidence interval for $p$: from 0.506 to 0.558. How does it relate to the one-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$?
options: It agrees: every value is above 0.5, as rejecting $H_0$ at 0.05 suggests
It disagrees, because the interval uses 90% confidence and the test used 5%
It disagrees, because the interval contains 0.532
It shows that 90% of adults support the four-day week

why.correct: A one-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ goes with a 90% interval (5% in each tail), and the two almost always agree. Every value in the interval is above 0.5, which agrees with rejecting $H_0: p = 0.5$ in favor of $p > 0.5$, and the interval also estimates how much above 0.5 the proportion is.
options: Right: the interval and the test tell the same story, and the interval adds a range for $p$.
A 90% interval leaves 5% in each tail, which is what goes with a one-sided test at 0.05.
Every interval contains its own sample proportion; what matters is whether it contains 0.5.
The 90% is the confidence level, not a share of adults.

items.q: A city says 30% of its bus riders pay with a phone app. A transit group thinks the share is higher. In a random sample of 600 riders, 207 use the app ($\hat{p} = 0.345$). Type the expression for the test statistic of $H_0: p = 0.30$ against $H_a: p > 0.30$, with values substituted.

mistakes.why: A test's standard deviation uses $p_0 = 0.30$, not $\hat{p}$: $\sqrt{0.30(0.70)/600}$.
Divide by $n = 600$ inside the square root.

items.q: For the bus-app test ($z = 2.41$, $H_a: p > 0.30$), find the p-value. Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is the area below $z = 2.41$. "Greater than" means the right tail.
That uses $\hat{p}$ in the standard deviation ($z = 2.32$). Use $p_0 = 0.30$.

why.correct: Right tail: $P(Z \ge 2.41) = 0.0081$. Technology gives 0.0081; Table A gives $1 - 0.9920 = 0.0080$.

items.q: State the conclusion of the bus-app test at $\alpha = 0.05$ (p-value 0.0081).

conclude.parameter: the true proportion of all the city's bus riders who pay with the app

options: There is convincing evidence
There is not convincing evidence
We have proven

why.1: A p-value of 0.0081 is below 0.05, so the evidence is convincing.

options: is greater than 0.30
is not equal to 0.30

why.1: The alternative was one-sided: greater than 0.30.
why.2: The test does not show the proportion equals the sample value.

options: that the true proportion of all the city's bus riders who pay with the app
that the 207 riders who use the app
that the proportion of the 600 sampled riders who pay with the app

why.1: The conclusion is about a proportion of all riders.
why.2: The sample proportion is known; the conclusion is about the population.

conclude.model: Because the p-value of 0.0081 is less than α = 0.05, we reject H0. There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of all the city's bus riders who pay with the app is greater than 0.30.

why.correct: Because $0.0081 < 0.05$, reject $H_0$: there is convincing evidence that the true proportion of all the city's bus riders who pay with the app is greater than 0.30.

items.q: A test of $H_0: p = 0.25$ against $H_a: p \ne 0.25$ gives a p-value of 0.38. Which conclusion is worded correctly?
options: We accept $H_0$: the true proportion is 0.25
We fail to reject $H_0$: not convincing evidence that $p \ne 0.25$
There is a 38% chance that the true proportion is 0.25
The data prove that the proportion is still 0.25, just as it was before

why.correct: Because $0.38 > 0.05$, fail to reject $H_0$, and say the evidence is not convincing for $H_a$. Never "accept" $H_0$ or say it is true.
options: A test never accepts $H_0$; a large p-value means the data are consistent with it, not that it is true.
Right: the decision, then evidence language about $H_a$.
A p-value is not the probability that $H_0$ is true.
Tests never prove; failing to reject only means the evidence was not strong enough.

items.q: A student wants to test whether more than 10% of a lake's 2,000 fish carry a parasite. She catches a random sample of 40 fish. What is the problem with a one-sample z test here?
options: $40(0.10) = 4$ is less than 10, so the normal model is not justified
40 is less than 30, so the sample is too small
40 is more than 10% of the 2,000 fish
Fish in a lake are not a population that a random sample can be drawn from

why.correct: Large counts with $p_0$: $np_0 = 40(0.10) = 4$, which is less than 10. The sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is skewed, so a p-value from the normal distribution may be inaccurate.
options: Right: large counts fails for successes.
For proportions, check successes and failures with $p_0$, not $n \ge 30$.
10% of 2,000 is 200, so 40 is well under it.
The problem says the sample is random; the issue is that only 4 parasite carriers are expected.

items.q: A 95% confidence interval for a proportion runs from 0.46 to 0.52. What would a two-sided test of $H_0: p = 0.50$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ conclude?
options: Reject $H_0$, because 0.49, the center, is not 0.50
Fail to reject $H_0$, because 0.50 is inside the interval
Reject $H_0$, because the interval includes values below 0.50
Nothing, because intervals and tests answer different questions

why.correct: A 95% interval and a two-sided test at 0.05 almost always agree (they differ only in rare borderline cases, because the test uses $p_0$ in its standard deviation). 0.50 is inside the interval, so it is plausible: the test would fail to reject $H_0$.
options: Being off the center is expected; what matters is that 0.50 is inside the interval.
Right: a plausible value is not ruled out by the matching test.
It also includes 0.50 itself, so 0.50 is plausible.
For the same data, a 95% interval and a two-sided test at 0.05 almost always agree about $p_0$.

items.q: Put the four steps of a significance test in order.
options: State: hypotheses, $\alpha$, and the parameter in context
Plan: name the procedure and check the conditions
Do: compute the test statistic and the p-value
Conclude: compare the p-value with $\alpha$ and state the conclusion in context

why.correct: State what you are testing, plan how (procedure and conditions), do the calculation, then conclude in context.
